Incorporating the SLOOS, the overall tone around policy and credit conditions skews more positive than initially assessed. While the FOMC kept rates at 0–0.25% and accelerated tapering amid elevated inflation and virus risks, banks broadly eased lending standards across residential real estate (including jumbo, QM and non-QM), HELOCs, consumer credit, credit cards, autos, and CRE; they also increased credit card limits and reduced auto loan rates. Demand was reported stronger for consumer loans and expected to strengthen for credit cards and C&I, with foreign banks noting stronger CRE demand alongside eased CRE standards. Offsetting factors include weaker reported demand in some categories (auto, C&I), unchanged standards in certain niches (government residential), and unchanged construction/land development demand. Net, SLOOS points to improving credit supply and resilient demand, reinforcing the “accommodative financial conditions” described in the statement but with pockets of softness. On balance, this nudges sentiment modestly higher.
